items.title: Finite indexed geometric site sets and duplicate handling
items.statement: A nonempty finite indexed site list of exact dyadic sites in R2 or R3 has stable integer identifiers; collapse unweighted duplicates by coordinate and weighted duplicates by coordinate-weight pair, retaining the least identifier. The ambient real field is Dedekind complete and ordered.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9
CGAL 6.3 User Manual, 3D Triangulations

items.title: A complete ordered field has cofinal canonical integers
items.statement: In any complete ordered field F with 1>0, every x in F is strictly exceeded by a canonical integer.

references.title: Truman, Bruckner, and Bruckner, Elementary Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Section 1.7, The Archimedean Property

items.title: The affine edge interpolant is the unique degree-one cardinal polynomial
items.statement: Over any field, distinct nodes a,b and values y0,y1 have the unique degree-at-most-one interpolant y0+(y1-y0)(X-a)/(b-a).

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9

items.title: Stable-id lexicographic lift perturbation for cocircular and power ties
items.statement: For a fixed finite universe of indexed sites, including any synthetic sites, perturb each lifted height by epsilon to the power two-to-the-rank of its stable id; use the same universe-wide ranks in every tuple and resolve an exact zero by the first nonzero coefficient.

references.title: Don Sheehy, Computational Geometry, Fall 2014, Lecture 22: Weighted Delaunay Triangulations
CGAL 6.3 User Manual, 3D Triangulations, Regular Triangulation

items.title: The lifted determinant records a power-sphere side
items.statement: For affinely independent base sites in dimension two or three and arbitrary dyadic weights, the determinant with lifted column norm-squared minus weight equals minus the base orientation determinant times the query power-distance difference from their common power sphere.

references.title: David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 13: Delaunay Triangulations: Incremental Construction
Don Sheehy, Computational Geometry, Fall 2014, Lecture 22: Weighted Delaunay Triangulations
CGAL 6.3 User Manual, 3D Triangulations, Regular Triangulation

items.title: A Voronoi vertex has a common empty circle of nearest sites
items.statement: If at least three distinct closed Voronoi cells meet at x, their sites are vertices of one empty circle centered at x and their convex hull is a polygon.

references.title: David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 11
Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9

items.title: Planar triangulations, Delaunay structures, and Voronoi cells
items.statement: For a finite deduplicated planar site set, define affine dimension, its lower-dimensional chain output, a triangulation of the convex hull, closed nearest-site Voronoi cells, their dual graph, weak empty-circle Delaunay faces, the convex-hull boundary convention, and the lexicographic tie convention for nonunique cocircular triangulations.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lectures 11–13

items.title: Three-dimensional Delaunay and weighted regular triangulations by lifting
items.statement: Lift each weighted site p with weight w to (p, norm-squared of p minus w) in R4; define the regular subdivision as the projection of the lower convex hull, the weight-zero Delaunay case, hidden sites, affine-dimension output, and a stable-id lexicographic lift refinement.

references.title: Don Sheehy, Computational Geometry, Fall 2014, Lecture 22: Weighted Delaunay Triangulations
CGAL 6.3 User Manual, 3D Triangulations, Regular Triangulation

items.title: The finite lexicographic lift tie-break is coherent
items.statement: For d=2 or 3 and a tuple of d+2 distinct sites with an affinely independent base, the fixed finite lexicographic lift resolves zero determinants coherently and preserves every nonzero constant sign.

references.title: Don Sheehy, Computational Geometry, Fall 2014, Lecture 22: Weighted Delaunay Triangulations
CGAL 6.3 User Manual, 3D Triangulations, Regular Triangulation

items.title: Barycentric point location, affine interpolation, and nearest-site queries
items.statement: On a nondegenerate simplex, define the unique affine barycentric coordinates, the vertex-data affine interpolant, exact point-in-cell status, outside-hull status, and the stable-id nearest-site Voronoi query.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lectures 11–13

items.title: Euler counting for a finite planar triangulation
items.statement: For n distinct planar sites of affine dimension two, k boundary sites, E edges and T triangular faces in any finite triangulation, 3T=2E-k and n-E+T=1; thus T=2n-2-k and E=3n-3-k.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 12

items.title: A dyadic supertriangle contains the sites and excludes every input circumcircle
items.statement: A dyadic supertriangle strictly contains any finite full-dimensional planar dyadic set and has vertices outside every input circumcircle; with general-position input, it can also make the augmented set general position.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, Sections 9.2–9.3
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 13

items.title: An illegal planar Delaunay flip strictly decreases lifted interpolation volume
items.statement: For a convex quadrilateral with a nonlegal diagonal, the triangulation using that diagonal has strictly larger integral of its piecewise-affine lifted-height interpolant than the flipped triangulation, using the common lexicographic lift to make cocircular ties strict.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, Section 9.2
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 13
Don Sheehy, Computational Geometry, Fall 2014, Lecture 22

items.title: Generic lower lifted facets project to a triangulation of the convex hull
items.statement: For a finite full-dimensional planar or 3D projected site set, the coherent formal lower simplices cover the convex hull, intersect in common faces, and have weakly empty original power spheres.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9
CGAL 6.3 User Manual, 3D Triangulations, The Delaunay and Regular Triangulations

items.title: A convex 4-polytope has at most m(m−3)/2 facets
items.statement: Every full-dimensional convex 4-polytope with m≥5 vertices has at most m(m−3)/2 facets.

references.title: CGAL 6.3 User Manual, 3D Triangulations, Complexity and Performance
Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9

items.title: Barycentric interpolation and nearest-site queries are correct
items.statement: Barycentric coordinates decide exact simplex membership and give the unique affine interpolant on each Delaunay cell; along each edge this is the unique degree-one cardinal interpolant, and a nearest-site query returns a minimizer with the stated inside- or outside-hull status.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 11

items.title: A planar triangulation has linearly many triangles and edges
items.statement: For n distinct planar sites of affine dimension two, every triangulation of their convex hull has 2n minus 2 minus k triangles and 3n minus 3 minus k edges, where k counts the sites on the hull boundary.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 13

items.title: Incremental planar Delaunay insertion with exact edge flips
items.statement:
Input is a finite indexed planar list of exact dyadic sites and optionally a prescribed insertion permutation. Collapse equal coordinates to the least stable identifier. If no permutation is supplied, use increasing stable-identifier order; otherwise require the permutation to list each deduplicated site exactly once. If the affine dimension is zero, return the single site; if it is one, sort by the first varying coordinate (use $x$ if it varies, otherwise $y$) and return the consecutive chain. These branches return no triangles.

For affine dimension two, run `CHOOSE-SUPERTRIANGLE(P,g)` before insertion, where $g=0$ in an ordinary batch run and $g=1$ when a caller requires the augmented general-position condition. Enumerate ordered triples of dyadic points by increasing height $H=0,1,2,\ldots$: represent each dyadic coordinate uniquely as $m/2^k$ with $k\ge0$ and either $k=0$ or odd $m$, and at height $H$ enumerate lexicographically the six coordinate representations with $|m|,k\le H$ and maximum $H$. For each candidate triple, reject coincident vertices or zero orientation; if its orientation is negative, swap the second and third vertices so it is counterclockwise. Reject it unless all input sites have strictly positive orientation against each of its three directed edges. For every noncollinear input triple and each candidate vertex, call [[alg-certified-dyadic-geometric-predicate]] for its exact orientation-normalized raw incircle sign and reject unless that sign is negative (outside). If $g=1$, test each input triple for zero orientation and each input four-site subset for zero raw incircle determinant; return `invalid-general-position-request` if either occurs. For each remaining candidate, also test every augmented triple for zero orientation and every augmented four-site subset for zero raw incircle determinant, rejecting that candidate if any test is zero. Return the first accepted triangle. The enumeration is deterministic and finite at each height; [[lem-large-delaunay-supertriangle-exists]] guarantees that an accepted candidate occurs for $g=0$, and also for $g=1$ under its general-position hypothesis. Assign the three synthetic vertices, in their enumerated order after the orientation correction, the consecutive integer identifiers immediately below the least input identifier. This fixes the universe $U$ and all lexicographic ranks before insertion. Initialize the current triangulation to the supertriangle and maintain its finite triangle list and edge incidences.

Expose the following state update `INSERT(p,L)`, where $p$ is a not-yet-inserted input site and $L$ is an optional location certificate. Its admissibility condition is that $p$ lies strictly inside the current triangulated hull. A face certificate names one current triangle $abc$ and is valid exactly when the three exact orientation tests put $p$ strictly in its interior. An edge certificate names an interior edge $uv$ and its two current incident triangles; it is valid exactly when $p$ lies strictly between $u$ and $v$ and those are the two triangles incident to $uv$. If a supplied certificate is invalid, return `invalid-location` without changing the triangulation. If $L$ is absent, scan the finite current triangle list in increasing lexicographic order of the sorted vertex identifiers. For each triangle $abc$, compute $s=\operatorname{sgn}\operatorname{orient}(a,b,c)$ and the three signs $s_{ab}=\operatorname{sgn}\operatorname{orient}(a,b,p)$, $s_{bc}=\operatorname{sgn}\operatorname{orient}(b,c,p)$, and $s_{ca}=\operatorname{sgn}\operatorname{orient}(c,a,p)$. If $ss_{ab},ss_{bc},ss_{ca}$ are all positive, use the face certificate for $abc$. If exactly one is zero and the other two are positive, use the edge certificate for that edge and its two incident triangles; if it is a hull edge, return `boundary-edge`. Two or more zero signs put $p$ at an existing vertex, contrary to the distinct-site input, and return `duplicate-vertex`. If the scan finds no containing face or interior edge, return `outside-hull`.

For a face certificate, replace its triangle by the three triangles joining $p$ to its edges. For an interior-edge certificate, replace its two incident triangles by the four triangles joining $p$ to the edge endpoints and the two opposite vertices. Then call `LEGALIZE(p,uv)` once on each distinct new edge $uv$ opposite $p$, in lexicographic order of its endpoint identifiers. In each call, order $u,v$ by stable identifier and let $w$ be the third vertex of the adjacent triangle. Compute the exact orientation determinant $O$ on rows $(u,v,w)$ and the raw lifted determinant sign $L$ on rows $(u,v,w,p)$ using [[alg-certified-dyadic-geometric-predicate]]. If $O=0$, return `degenerate-base`. If $L\ne0$, set the normalized sign to $\operatorname{sgn}(O)L$. If $L=0$, take the sign $L_{\rm lex}$ selected from the common formal height perturbation of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]] on the same row order and set the normalized sign to $\operatorname{sgn}(O)L_{\rm lex}$. A positive normalized sign means illegal; a negative sign means legal; zero is treated as legal. Boundary edges have no adjacent triangle and are legal. If an edge is illegal, test strict convexity with exact orientations: both $p,w$ must lie on opposite sides of $uv$, and $u,v$ must lie on opposite sides of $pw$. If either product of the corresponding two orientation signs is not negative, return `invalid-triangulation`. Otherwise flip $uv$ to $pw$, record the replacement event, and recursively call `LEGALIZE(p,uw)` and `LEGALIZE(p,wv)` in lexicographic order. Each face split, edge split, and flip records its removed triangles, created triangles, and overlap map: one-to-three for a face split, two-to-two-within-each-old-face for an edge split, and both new triangles for each old face at a flip. `INSERT` returns these events in execution order with the updated triangulation. A batch run calls `INSERT(p,none)` for each site in the chosen permutation, discards the event lists, halts with any returned status, and otherwise returns the remaining triangles and their edges after deleting triangles incident to synthetic vertices.

The exact raw predicate and its tie-break are separate: [[alg-certified-dyadic-geometric-predicate]] returns exact raw signs including zero; a zero nondegenerate-base sphere test is resolved by the common formal height perturbation in this algorithm. The procedure never chooses or evaluates a numerical $\varepsilon$. A degenerate base is reported as `degenerate-base` and is not flipped.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, Sections 9.2–9.3
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 13

items.title: Finite exact 3D Delaunay and regular lower-hull cavity repair
items.statement: For dyadic weighted 3D sites, collapse exact coordinate-weight duplicates, report lower affine dimension directly, record degenerate projected four-site bases, enumerate exact lower tetrahedra at every prefix, repair the set of violated lower cells on insertion, and report hidden sites.

references.title: Don Sheehy, Computational Geometry, Fall 2014, Lecture 22: Weighted Delaunay Triangulations
CGAL 6.3 User Manual, 3D Triangulations, Regular Triangulations and Conflict Zones

items.title: Randomized planar point location by a history DAG
items.statement:
Assume a finite full-dimensional planar site set in general position: no three input sites are collinear and no four are cocircular. Choose the augmented dyadic supertriangle by calling `CHOOSE-SUPERTRIANGLE(P,1)` from [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]], so the full augmented set has no three collinear sites and no four cocircular sites. Fix the common tie ranks before processing.

Draw one permutation uniformly from all $n!$ permutations of the distinct input sites. Initialize the fixed-universe supertriangle and current triangulation as in [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]], and maintain a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose leaves correspond one-to-one with current triangulation triangles. Initially the DAG has one leaf for the supertriangle.

For each next site $p$, start at the root. At each node, order its child triangles lexicographically by their sorted vertex identifiers and test each child by the same three signed-orientation containment tests used by `INSERT` in [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]]. Descend to the unique child containing $p$ until reaching a current leaf $T$. Under the augmented general-position condition, $p$ lies in the interior of a unique triangle at every stage; the located leaf therefore supplies the face certificate `face(T)`. Call `INSERT(p,face(T))` from [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]]. The update verifies that certificate, uses it without a triangle scan, and returns the ordered replacement events. Process those events in order: for a face split, replace the old leaf by pointers to its three new triangle leaves; for an interior-edge split, replace each of the two old leaves by pointers to the two new triangles whose interiors meet that old triangle; for a flip, point each of the two old leaves to both new triangle leaves. Each event names the triangles and overlap map as specified by the insertion procedure. A leaf replaced later is treated in the same way, so the graph remains acyclic and its current leaves correspond exactly to the current triangulation. The insertion procedure also accepts an interior-edge certificate from callers whose admissible inputs permit edge hits; this randomized variant's general-position condition excludes that case. Each internal node has at most three children. After construction, remove synthetic-vertex triangles for the returned Delaunay triangulation; the history DAG is the insertion-time point-location structure.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, Sections 9.3–9.4
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 13

items.title: Exact planar insertion terminates with a weak empty-circle triangulation
items.statement: For every nonempty finite indexed dyadic planar set, exact insertion and recursive local edge flips terminate; each full-dimensional prefix is the common formal lift lower triangulation, and dimensions zero or one return the defined site or chain.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, Sections 9.2–9.3
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 13

items.title: Exact 3D lower-hull insertion covers the hull and terminates
items.statement: On the full-dimensional projected branch, finite exact lower-facet enumeration and cavity repair terminate, cover the convex hull by common-face tetrahedra with weakly empty power spheres, identify hidden sites, and report degenerate bases; lower-dimensional inputs return a named status.

references.title: Don Sheehy, Computational Geometry, Fall 2014, Lecture 22: Weighted Delaunay Triangulations
CGAL 6.3 User Manual, 3D Triangulations, The Delaunay and Regular Triangulations

items.title: Uniform random insertion gives expected O(n log n) location work
items.statement: For a full-dimensional planar input and augmented supertriangle in general position, a uniform random insertion order gives expected O(n log n) total history-DAG point-location work and expected O(n) triangle creation and DAG storage; a conservative worst case is O(n^3).

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, Sections 9.3–9.4, Theorem 9.12 and Lemma 9.13
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 13

items.title: Three-dimensional Delaunay and regular output size is quadratic
items.statement: For n at least 4 weighted sites of projected affine dimension three, the fixed formal lift returns at most n(n minus 3)/2 Delaunay or regular tetrahedra, hence O(n squared), with no mesh-quality guarantee.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9
CGAL 6.3 User Manual, 3D Triangulations, Complexity and Performance

title: Delaunay triangulations and voronoi computation — Examples

items.title: A cocircular four-site tie selects the stable-id diagonal
items.statement: For the unit square with ids A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4 and zero weights, the four unperturbed lifted points are coplanar, the lexicographic height perturbation selects diagonal BD, and both selected triangles satisfy the original weak empty-circle condition.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9
Don Sheehy, Computational Geometry, Fall 2014, Lecture 22

items.title: Collinear and duplicate sites return a canonical chain
items.statement: For the finite input (0,0),(1,0),(1,0),(2,0) with distinct ids, duplicate collapse keeps the least id at (1,0), affine dimension is one, and the lower-dimensional Delaunay output is the ordered two-edge chain.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, Section 9.1
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 11

items.title: A scattered affine interpolant on one Delaunay cell
items.statement: On the Delaunay triangle with vertices (0,0),(2,0),(0,2) and vertex data 0,2,2, the query (1/2,1/2) has barycentric weights 1/2,1/4,1/4 and affine interpolated value 1.

references.title: Mark de Berg et al., Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9
David M. Mount, CMSC 754 Computational Geometry, Lecture 11
